title: Designing a Public API / Library Surface
summary: Deciding what a class or module exposes to callers you don't control, and how to change it later without breaking them.

slides.markdown:
Once a class or module ships to callers you don't control, every public method, field, and type becomes a promise you have to keep — someone, somewhere, is already calling it the way it exists today. The real skill isn't designing the perfect surface up front; it's designing one you can still change later without breaking everyone.

Think of a public API like a rented storefront: customers only interact with the front window and the door — what happens in the stockroom is yours to rearrange freely, as long as the storefront stays put.

This topic covers minimal surface area, what backward compatibility actually requires, and how to retire an API without breaking the callers who trusted it.

slides.sectionTitle: Minimal surface area: expose the smallest contract that solves the caller's problem
slides.markdown:
The smallest public surface that solves the caller's problem is also the easiest one to maintain — every public method, field, or type you expose is something you now have to support forever, or explicitly break. A class with three public methods and twelve private helpers is far easier to evolve than one where all fifteen are public, even if callers only ever use three.

The habit: default everything to private or internal, and promote something to public only when a real caller needs it. It's much cheaper to widen a surface later — add a method — than to narrow one, which means coordinating a breaking change across every consumer.

A generous public surface feels helpful today and becomes the exact thing that blocks tomorrow's refactor.

slides.sectionTitle: Public vs internal: what belongs in the API vs what's an implementation detail masquerading as one
slides.markdown:
Not everything that's technically reachable is meant to be part of the contract. A class might expose a `getConnectionPool()` method purely so its own subclasses or same-package helpers can use it — that's an **implementation detail masquerading as public**, and callers who find it will use it, contract or not.

The test: would you feel free to rename, remove, or change the behavior of this member without warning anyone? If yes, it shouldn't be public — mark it internal or package-private so tooling and readers both know it isn't a promise. If no, it's genuinely public, and needs the same care as any other contract.

Callers will eventually depend on anything reachable, whether you intended it as an API or not — visibility keywords are the only real fence.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: a library's public surface vs its internals, and where the real seam is
slides.markdown:
<<< Image: a library drawn as a box; a thin outer ring labelled "public surface" contains a handful of methods with arrows pointing out to external caller code; the much larger interior labelled "internals" contains helper classes and private methods with no arrows crossing the boundary >>>

A library's real complexity usually lives in a large internal layer — helper classes, private state, implementation choices — that callers never see and shouldn't need to. The public surface is deliberately thin: a handful of methods and types that callers actually call.

The seam that matters for compatibility isn't the whole codebase, it's this ring — everything inside it can be rewritten freely; everything crossing it needs a compatibility plan.

slides.sectionTitle: Backwards compatibility: additive-safe changes vs breaking changes
slides.markdown:
Not every change to a public API costs the same. **Additive-safe changes** extend the surface without touching what already works: adding a new method, adding an optional parameter with a default, adding a new field to a response object. **Breaking changes** remove or alter something callers already depend on: renaming a method, changing a parameter's type, removing a field, or changing what a method returns for the same input.

| | Additive-safe | Breaking |
|---|---|---|
| Existing callers | Unaffected, keep compiling and working | Fail to compile or behave differently |
| Example | New optional parameter with a default | Changing a return type |
| Requires | Nothing extra | A major version bump, deprecation window, or migration guide |

**How to decide:** before shipping a change, ask whether an existing caller's code, unmodified, still compiles and behaves the same. If the answer is no for even one realistic caller, treat it as breaking.

slides.sectionTitle: Deprecation as a process: marking, documenting, and giving callers a migration path before removal
slides.markdown:
Removing a public API without warning breaks callers who did nothing wrong — they used a documented method as intended. **Deprecation** is the process that lets you retire something responsibly: mark it with a reason and the replacement to use, document the migration path, and give callers a real window — often measured in minor versions or months, not days — before you actually remove it.

A good deprecation notice answers three things: what's going away, what to use instead, and by when. Skipping any of the three just moves the breakage from "documented and expected" to "a surprise support ticket."

The removal itself should only ever happen in a major version bump, after the deprecation window has genuinely passed.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: adding a parameter to a public method without breaking existing callers (overload vs default vs builder)
Semantic versioning as a promise to callers, not a formality
slides.markdown:
**Semantic versioning** (`MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`) is a promise to callers, encoded in a number: bump `PATCH` for a bug fix that changes no contract, `MINOR` for adding backward-compatible functionality, `MAJOR` for anything that breaks existing callers. A caller who pins `^2.3.0` is trusting that any `2.x` release won't break their code — that trust is the entire point of the scheme.

The promise only holds if you're disciplined about classifying changes correctly. Shipping a breaking change as a `MINOR` bump because it "seemed small" doesn't just break the caller who upgrades; it teaches every caller of your library that version numbers can't be trusted, which erodes the value of the whole scheme for everyone downstream.

When in doubt about whether a change is breaking, treat it as breaking — the cost of an unnecessary major bump is far lower than the cost of a broken promise.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: exposing a mutable internal object and losing control of your own invariants
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Returning my internal list directly is fine — it saves a copy."

**Why it's wrong:** once a caller holds a direct reference to your internal collection, they can mutate it — add, remove, reorder — and your class's invariants (say, that orders stay sorted by date) silently break from outside code you never see. The class thinks it owns and controls that list; it no longer does. This is the same failure as poor **encapsulation**: state that should only change through the class's own methods is now reachable directly.

**Correct model:** return an immutable view or a defensive copy from any public accessor that exposes internal mutable state. It costs a copy, but it's the difference between "my invariants hold because I enforce them" and "my invariants hold as long as no caller ever mutates what I handed them."
